chunks: First: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from al-Salih ibn Sa'id, from Yunus, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who was angry with his wife, or a woman who was angry with her husband, and one of them killed the other. He said: There is no qisas (retaliation) upon them if they are considered trustworthy (not intending death). If they are suspected, it is incumbent upon them to swear an oath to God that they did not intend killing. Second: As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammam, from al-Halabi, and Hisham, and al-Nadr, and Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Ibn Mukkan, all from Sulayman ibn Khalid, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he was asked about a man who was angry with a woman and claimed she died from his anger, he said: The diya (blood money) is complete and the man is not killed, so it does not contradict the first report, because we interpret the first report as meaning that only qisas was negated for them, but diya was not negated. The suspicion is removed by each of them swearing that he did not intend to kill his partner, then the diya becomes incumbent upon him.

key_terms.عَنَفَ: To be angry or lose temper

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling when a husband or wife kills the other in a fit of anger?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi synthesizes two reports in this chapter to distinguish between qisas (retribution) and diya (blood money) in cases of spousal homicide driven by anger (urfah). He clarifies that while a trustworthy spouse is exempt from execution upon swearing they did not intend death, the obligation of full diya remains, resolving apparent contradictions by attributing the first report's silence on diya to its specific focus on negating qisas. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle of distinguishing between intent for killing versus intent for causing death, ensuring financial compensation even when capital punishment is waived.
